The man's grip was weak, his fingers cold and trembling despite the heat radiating from the stove. He did not meet Scotty's eyes but stared instead at the bacon, watching the thin strips curl and spit in their own rendered fat. Three slices. Not enough for one hungry man, let alone two.

"I had given up," Scotty continued, his voice barely above a whisper. "When I saw you out there in the snow, I thought you were another one of them. The ones who don't get up again."

He turned then, and the firelight caught the hollows of his face, the sharp edges of his cheekbones pressing against pale skin. He looked like a man who had been dying slowly for a long time and had grown accustomed to it.

"Sit down," he said. "We'll split it three ways. Three for you, three for me." He laughed, a short, bitter sound. "I'm joking. God knows there's nothing funny about it."

"We'd have had beans this morning if
I hadn't shook dice with him last night." He nodded toward the bearded man,
who was cutting open the top of a can. "He won!"

"My God!" began Roscoe.

He didn't finish. Scotty turned the meat, and added:

"He won a square meal off me yesterday--a quarter of a pound of bacon. Day
before that he won Henry's last can of beans. He's got his share under his
blanket over there, and swears he'll shoot any one who goes to monkeying
with his bed--so you'd better fight shy of it. Thompson--he isn't up
yet--chose the whisky for _his_ share, so you'd better fight shy of him,
too. Henry and I'll divvy up with you."
pair.prefix:
He saw that there were three thin
slices of bacon in the frying pan, and it struck him that it would be bad
taste to reveal a starvation appetite in the face of such famine. He came
up, limping, and stood on the other side of the stove from Scotty.

"You saved my life," he said, holding out a hand. "Will you shake?"

Scotty shook hands limply.

"It's h--l," he said in a low voice.

source_document.title: The Grizzly King by James Oliver Curwood
